scene.testo: Three German prisoners walked into the Maine woods in March 1945, certain they could reach the ocean and sail to Argentina. They made it about thirty miles. One of them later helped America reach the moon.

Why would prisoners who were fed, paid, and housed decently risk a deadly winter march through the wilderness? And why did they believe a homemade compass would carry them across a hundred miles of frozen country?
The answer is not cruelty. It is not hunger. It is something far stranger, and it begins with a guard asleep under a fir tree. But first, you need to see where this happened.
March 7th, 1945. A frozen lake in the North Woods of Maine. A crew of German prisoners of war is cutting ice. Their American guard sits down beneath a fir tree. His eyes close. He sleeps.
Three young prisoners look at each other. They look at the guard. They look at the forest. Then they walk into the trees. Nobody calls out. Nobody follows. The woods close behind them.

They were Franz Keller, eighteen, Horst Schlueter, nineteen, and Anton Gabe, twenty. They carried snowshoes they had built themselves, and a compass made from a sewing needle and the lid of a can of peaches.
Their plan was simple, and almost absurd. Reach the Atlantic coast. Board a ship. Sail to Argentina. Between them and that ocean stood the Maine woods in winter. They had no idea what that meant.
To understand how three teenagers ended up on that frozen lake, we must go back to 1944. America was at war on two oceans, and it had a problem. It was running out of workers.
The young men of Maine were overseas. Yet the paper mills still needed pulpwood. Wartime America ran on paper. Ration books, shipping crates, and the boxes that carried ammunition all depended on it.

At the same time, the United States held hundreds of thousands of German prisoners of war, captured in North Africa and Europe and shipped across the Atlantic. The answer to both problems seemed obvious. Send the prisoners to work.
Maine took in nearly four thousand of them. The main camp stood at Houlton, near the Canadian border. Smaller branch camps spread across the state, each one built close to the timber.
One of them stood at the north end of Spencer Lake, in a township called Hobbstown, deep in the woods west of Moosehead Lake. The paper company Hollingsworth and Whitney built it for the war.
Twenty-two buildings. Barbed wire. Guard towers. It was designed for two hundred fifty men. In July 1944, the first prisoners arrived by train at Bingham and rode the rest of the way into the forest.
By March 1945, the camp held three hundred ten men. The nearest public road was twelve miles away. In practice, the forest itself was the fence. Everyone in the camp knew it. Almost everyone.
Life there was not what a German soldier expected from an enemy. Under the Geneva Convention, prisoners were fed like American soldiers and paid for their labor in camp coupons.
They cut pulpwood all day. In the evenings, there were classes, music, and sports. Across Maine, farmers and foremen were surprised by how hard the prisoners worked, and some came to respect them.

But a prison in the woods is still a prison. And the camp commander, Major William Marshall, held an unusual attitude. By the accounts that survive, he more or less dared his prisoners to try to escape.
Three of them decided to take him up on it. They did not rush. They prepared all winter, quietly, in the evenings, in the barracks, while the snow piled higher against the walls.

They saved food from their rations. They hid sugar under their clothes. They made snowshoes from boards and rail ties, and harnesses from leather belts and stovepipe wire. They made knives. On the work detail, they already had axes.

From a French Canadian woodcutter, they obtained a map. And they built the compass. A sewing needle, magnetized with an electrical coil, balanced on the tin top of a peach can. It was their only guide.
The route was about one hundred miles to the coast. Then a freighter. Then Argentina, a country still friendly to Germany, where they could wait out the war in the sun. On paper, it looked possible.
On March 7th, the ice-cutting crew went out onto the lake. The guard sat down under his tree and fell asleep. Keller, Schlueter, and Gabe walked away. Nobody noticed until evening roll call.
Major Marshall called for help. The next morning, about thirty men arrived. The Maine State Police, the Somerset County Sheriff, the Maine Warden Service, and the FBI. They brought bloodhounds.
It became one of the largest manhunts in the history of Maine. Three planes flew low over Spencer Lake for two days, searching for tracks in the snow, for smoke, for anything. They found nothing.
Out in the trees, the escapees were learning what the Maine woods are in March. They moved at night. By day, they slept in shelters dug out of the snow and roofed with pine boughs.
The snow was deep. The nights were well below freezing. And the peach can compass could point north, but it could not show them what stood in their way. Rivers. Spencer Stream. The Dead River.
In March, under thin ice, the water runs black and fast. Three men on homemade snowshoes could not cross it. So they walked along the banks, looking for a way over. The rivers decided their route.
On the third day of the search, the sheriff deputized a man named Bill Hall. Hall was a hermit. Since 1932, he had lived alone in an old trapper's cabin in those woods, avoiding people and publicity.

But he knew the country better than any warden. He looked at the map and thought about the rivers. Men on foot with no boat could not cross them in March. They would have to follow the water downstream.
And the water led to one place. West Forks, a small logging settlement about thirty miles from the camp. Go to West Forks, Bill Hall told the wardens. It was the right answer.

On March 12th, 1945, five days after the escape, two game wardens found a makeshift lean-to near West Forks. Inside were three cold, hungry German prisoners. The wardens took their axes and walked them to a country store.

They had covered about thirty of their hundred miles. The ocean and Argentina were exactly as far away as ever. When the army questioned them, the answers surprised everyone. Nobody had mistreated them.

One said Major Marshall had challenged them to try. We wanted to show him it is possible to escape. Another gave a more Maine reason. He did not want another summer of mosquitoes, black flies, and no-see-ums.

Bill Hall never received public credit. That was how he wanted it. He went back to his cabin. The three young men went back behind the wire. Franz Keller spent three weeks in solitary confinement at Houlton.

But his story did not end there. Back in camp, the eighteen-year-old who had built a compass from a peach can took a correspondence course in astronomy from the University of Maine. The war ended that May.

The Spencer Lake camp closed in April 1946, and its prisoners went home to a Germany in ruins. Then, in 1957, Franz Keller returned, this time as an engineer. He worked on NASA's Apollo program, and in 1961 became an American citizen. The boy who steered by a needle helped steer America to the moon.

descrizione:
In March 1945, three young German prisoners of war walked away from a camp in the Maine woods, planning to reach the Atlantic coast and sail to Argentina. This documentary tells the true story of the Spencer Lake escape, the Maine manhunt, the hermit who guessed their route, and the surprising life of Franz Keller.

Drawing on documented accounts of German POW camps in Maine, the video explains why prisoners were sent to cut pulpwood, how the Hobbstown camp worked, and what the escapees said when questioned about their motives.
